prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All my life I was face to face with her, at meal-times, by the fire, even in the ultimate intimacies of the bed. You could have asked, then, for information about her? There was a room apart she kept herself in, teasing me by leading me to its glass door, only to confront me with my reflection. I learned from her even so. Walking her shore I found things cast up from her depths that spoke to me of another order, worshipper as I was of untamed nature. She fetched her treasures from art’s storehouse: pieces of old lace, delicate as frost; china from a forgotten period; a purse more valuable than anything it could contain. Coming in from the fields with my offering of flowers I found her garden had forestalled me in providing civilities for my desk. ‘Tell me about life,’ I would say, ‘you who were its messenger in the delivery of our child.’ Her eyes had a fine shame, remembering her privacy being invaded from further off than she expected. ‘Do you think death is the end?’ frivolously I would ask her. I recall now the swiftness of its arrival wrenching her lip down, and how the upper remained firm, reticent as the bud that is the precursor of the flower.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The narrator lived in constant physical intimacy with a woman yet remained unable to fully understand her inner life.
- She guarded her privacy, revealing only indirect glimpses of herself that often reflected the narrator back upon himself.
- The narrator learned about her through the refined objects and artistic treasures she gathered.
- Her cultivated sensibility often anticipated and surpassed his own offerings drawn from untamed nature.
- Memories of childbirth and death exposed her vulnerability, restraint, and awareness of life’s deepest mysteries.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A husband reflects on his lifelong inability to fully know his wife, approaching her mystery through their shared intimacies, her treasured objects, and questions about birth, life, and death. Her subtle, guarded responses reveal a private inner world and foreshadow her sudden death, underscoring the limits of intimacy and understanding.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: All, You, There

outputs.L1:
All my life, I was face to face with her—at mealtimes, by the fire, even in the ultimate intimacies of the bed. Could you, then, have asked me for information about her? She kept herself in a room apart, teasing me by leading me to its glass door, only to confront me with my own reflection. Even so, I learned from her. Walking her shore, I found things cast up from her depths that spoke to me of another order, worshipper as I was of untamed nature. She drew her treasures from art’s storehouse: pieces of old lace, delicate as frost; china from a forgotten period; a purse more valuable than anything it could contain. Coming in from the fields with my offering of flowers, I found that her garden had forestalled me, already providing civilities for my desk.

“Tell me about life,” I would say, “you who were its messenger in the delivery of our child.” Her eyes held a fine shame as she remembered her privacy being invaded from further off than she had expected. “Do you think death is the end?” I would ask her frivolously. I recall now the swiftness of its arrival, wrenching her lower lip downward, and how the upper remained firm—reticent as the bud that precedes the flower.
outputs.L2:
Throughout my existence she was constantly before me—across the table, beside the hearth, and in the deepest closeness of our shared bed. Yet could anyone have questioned me and truly learned who she was? She inhabited a private chamber within herself. She would lure me toward its transparent entrance, but when I looked through, I saw only my own image staring back.

Still, she taught me. As I wandered along the edge of her being, I discovered objects risen from hidden depths, signs of a realm beyond my own devotion to wild nature. Her riches came from the treasury of art: antique lace as intricate as ice crystals, porcelain belonging to some vanished age, and a handbag worth more than whatever might be placed inside it. When I returned from the countryside carrying flowers for her, I discovered that her cultivated garden had already supplied the graceful arrangement intended for my writing table.

“Explain life to me,” I would ask, “since you served as its envoy when our child was born.” A delicate embarrassment entered her eyes as she remembered how her privacy had been breached from a greater distance than she had anticipated.

“Do you believe death finishes everything?” I would inquire lightly. Now I remember how abruptly death came: it dragged one corner of her lower lip downward, while the upper lip stayed composed and withholding, closed like the bud that appears before the blossom.
outputs.L3:
The narrator lived in constant physical intimacy with the woman, sharing her daily presence and the closeness of her body, yet he remained unable to fully penetrate the mystery of her inner life. Familiarity did not lead to complete understanding. Instead, her thoughts and emotions seemed to remain protected behind an invisible boundary, reminding him that even the deepest intimacy cannot entirely erase the distance between two people.

She guarded her privacy carefully and rarely revealed herself directly. When she did offer glimpses of her inner world, they were often oblique, conveyed through gestures, choices, or moments of silence rather than explicit confession. These partial revelations frequently reflected the narrator back upon himself. In trying to interpret her, he became more conscious of his own desires, limitations, and assumptions.

He therefore learned about her indirectly, especially through the refined objects and artistic treasures she collected. Her possessions expressed dimensions of her personality that words could not: her taste, discipline, imagination, and responsiveness to beauty. Each carefully chosen object served as evidence of a rich, cultivated sensibility, allowing the narrator to approach her through the aesthetic world she created around herself.

Her sensitivity often anticipated and surpassed his own attempts to delight or impress her. Even when he brought her offerings drawn from wild, untamed nature, she seemed already to understand their beauty more deeply than he did. Her response transformed these gifts, revealing meanings and subtleties he had not recognized. Rather than simply receiving what he offered, she refined and enlarged his perception of it.

Yet it was in memories of childbirth and death that her deepest vulnerability became most visible. These experiences brought her into contact with the fundamental mysteries of existence: creation, suffering, loss, and mortality. Even then, however, she responded with restraint rather than open self-disclosure. Her composure did not diminish the intensity of her feeling; instead, it suggested a profound awareness of realities too powerful to be fully expressed. Through these memories, the narrator glimpsed both her fragility and her strength, while recognizing that the essential core of her being would always remain partly beyond his reach.
outputs.L4:
For most of our marriage, I believed that knowing another person was a matter of accumulation. Years would gather into certainty: breakfasts shared, illnesses endured, journeys taken, quarrels settled, nights spent sleeping within reach of the same lamp. I thought each intimacy would reveal something permanent about my wife, until at last nothing essential remained hidden.

Instead, the longer we lived together, the more clearly I sensed the distance within her.

It was not coldness. She was affectionate, sometimes playful, and attentive to the smallest changes in my mood. She knew when I wanted to speak and when I preferred silence. Yet when I tried to offer her the same attention, I often found myself standing before a closed door.

I approached her through the objects she loved. There was a silver-backed mirror that had belonged to her mother, though its glass was clouded and she rarely used it. A blue bowl, chipped along the rim, followed us from our first apartment to our last house. In a drawer she kept old train tickets tied with thread, a child’s red mitten, several letters without envelopes, and a smooth white stone she had picked up beside the sea.

“Why these?” I asked once.

She turned the stone in her palm.

“Because I kept them,” she said.

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It may be the only answer.”

She smiled, but the smile warned me not to press. I imagined each object attached to some hidden moment—a grief, a promise, a betrayal—but whenever I tried to make a story from them, she corrected me gently.

“No,” she would say. “It wasn’t like that.”

Then she would refuse to say how it had been.

At night, when darkness made confession seem possible, I asked about her childhood. Did she remember being born? Of course not, she said. Did she remember the first time she understood that she was alive?

She considered this more seriously.

“I remember lying under a table,” she said. “There was sunlight on the floor, and dust moving through it. I could hear adults talking, but I couldn’t understand the words. I knew they had forgotten I was there.”

“And that made you feel alive?”

“It made me feel separate.”

I wanted to ask whether she had felt separate ever since, even from me. Instead, I touched her shoulder. She covered my hand with hers, as if to comfort me for a question I had not spoken.

There were times when I thought her body told me what her voice would not. I knew the thin scar near her knee, the faint pulse at her throat, the way she curled toward warmth in her sleep. I knew how her breathing changed before she cried and how she pressed her lips together when she was angry. These seemed like forms of knowledge beyond language.

But the body, too, had its privacy. Pain could inhabit it without announcing itself. Memory could tighten a hand or darken a face and leave no explanation behind. Even in our closest embraces, I sometimes felt that she was listening to something far away.

Once I asked whether she was afraid of death.

She looked at me with mild surprise.

“Not of being dead.”

“Then of what?”

“Of leaving in the middle of something.”

“What something?”

“My life, I suppose.”

I laughed because the answer seemed circular. She did not laugh.

“And you?” she asked.

“I’m afraid of losing you.”

“That isn’t the same as being afraid of death.”

“It will be, if you die first.”

She lowered her eyes. “Perhaps.”

That word stayed with me. At the time, it sounded almost careless. Later, I would remember it as prophecy.

Her death came suddenly, on an ordinary morning. There had been no farewell disguised as tenderness, no final explanation, no arrangement of treasured objects into a message I might decipher afterward. She drank half a cup of tea, complained that the room was too warm, and stood to open a window. Before she reached it, she collapsed.

For years I had imagined that death would reveal her—that the sealed rooms of her nature might open at last, if only through the things she left behind. Instead, her absence made everything less certain.

I examined the letters in the drawer. They were affectionate but incomplete. I held the child’s mitten, though I never learned whose it had been. I took the white stone back to the sea and stood among thousands like it, unable to find any reason she had chosen that one.

The blue bowl remained on the kitchen shelf. Sometimes, in the early light, its chipped edge appeared almost luminous. I would remember her hands lifting it, washing it, setting it down. Such gestures had once seemed too ordinary to notice. Now they were all I had.

Gradually, I understood that I had mistaken intimacy for possession. I had wanted her memories arranged so I could enter them, her silences translated into words I could approve, her mystery reduced to a story in which I had a place. But she had belonged first to herself.

Perhaps that was what she had meant when she spoke of lying beneath the table, watching dust in sunlight and realizing that she was separate. Birth was not merely an arrival into the world; it was an arrival into solitude. Love could cross that solitude, could warm and illuminate it, but could never abolish it. Death did not create the distance between us. It only made the distance visible.

I still speak to her sometimes. I ask the questions I once withheld and repeat the ones she never answered. In imagination, she smiles her guarded smile.

It may be the only answer, she says.

And now, at last, I do not press her.
outputs.L5:
### All You Need Is There

Sometimes, we search everywhere for answers—through distant places, unfamiliar faces, and endless possibilities. Yet all you truly need may already be there: in the quiet strength you carry, the people who stand beside you, and the hope that returns each morning. Pause, look around, and trust yourself. Not everything is easy to see, but all the courage, love, and possibility you need is there.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical first-person monologue in which a widower reflects on how little he truly knew his wife despite their lifelong intimacy.
counterfactuals.output:
After she died, I found a blue button in the pocket of her winter coat.

It belonged to nothing I remembered. Not the navy dress she wore to our daughter’s wedding, nor the old cardigan she kept mending at the elbows, nor any blouse I had ever unfastened in the dark. It was a small, ordinary thing, scratched around the rim, with a loop of black thread still clinging to its eye.

I held it in my palm and understood, suddenly, that my wife had been full of rooms I had never entered.

We were married fifty-three years. I knew how she took her tea, how she slept with one foot outside the blanket, how she went quiet before rain. I knew the faint white scar beneath her chin, though I could never remember whether she said it came from a bicycle or a fall from the pear tree. I knew the sound of her key in the front door. I could tell, from the way she set down her handbag, whether the day had wounded her.

Or I believed I could.

There is an arrogance in long love. We say, I know you, when we mean, I have grown accustomed to your weather. We mistake the pattern of a life for its depths. I knew her seasons, yes—the bright impatience of her youth, the summer of children, the long autumn when we buried our parents and began speaking softly about our own bodies. But what did she dream beneath all that weather? What old name did she sometimes hear in a crowd? What wish did she fold away so neatly that even she forgot where she had put it?

In the weeks after the funeral, I opened drawers like a thief.

There were ticket stubs from a town I had never visited with her. A photograph of three girls standing ankle-deep in a river, their skirts lifted, their faces turned away. A recipe written in someone else’s hand, with *too much cinnamon* added in her small, slanting script. In the back of her sewing box, beneath the needles and chalk, I found a list of birds: linnet, kestrel, redwing, tern. Some were checked. Some were not.

I had not known she kept account of birds.

How many times had she looked up while I went on looking forward?

This is the grief that comes after grief: first you mourn the body, then the stranger who lived inside it. I miss her hand on my shoulder. I miss the warm hollow she left in the bed. But I also miss the woman I never thought to ask about—the girl in the river, the watcher of kestrels, the keeper of a button from some vanished coat.

Perhaps she did not know me either. Perhaps that is mercy. She knew my habits, my temper, the jokes I repeated and the fears I disguised as practical concerns. But there were corridors in me where even her footsteps never sounded. Love did not make us transparent. It made us brave enough to remain mysterious beside one another.

Still, I wish I had asked better questions.

Not, Did you lock the door? Not, What time will you be home? Not even, Are you happy?—that blunt, impossible question. I should have asked: What did you see today that you could not explain? Which life, besides this one, called to you? When you were silent beside me, where did you go?

Now I speak to her in the kitchen while the kettle climbs toward its whistle. I tell her I found the button. I tell her a redwing came to the garden, though I may have named it wrong. I tell her I am sorry for all the evenings I sat beside her, believing nearness was the same as knowing.

The dead do not answer, but they alter the silence.

Sometimes I imagine her listening with that half-smile she wore when I had finally arrived at something she had understood for years. Then the house grows still around me, immense and intimate, and I feel how love endures—not as knowledge, not as possession, but as wonder.

She was my wife.

She was my life.

And she was never only mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a modernist prose passage about marriage, privacy, childbirth, art, nature, and death, using rich metaphors and an elegiac tone.
counterfactuals.output:
Marriage was a house built partly of doors. Some opened inward, onto the shared rooms—the kettle’s small weather, the books leaning shoulder to shoulder, the bed with its pale republic of sleep. Others remained locked, not from cruelty but from necessity. Each carried a private country beneath the ribs, with its own ruined chapels, its own language of rain. Love did not abolish these borders. It stood at them quietly, holding a lamp.

When the child came, the house seemed to break open. Dawn entered everywhere. Pain, which had been a red animal pacing the body, suddenly became a passage; and through it arrived this wet, astonished creature, clenched around its first breath. She held the infant and felt time divide like a cell: before, after; self, other; terror, devotion. Her husband wept by the window, useless and radiant, while outside the pear tree scattered white petals over the lawn, as if spring had mistaken suffering for a wedding.

Afterward, she returned to her painting. Yet the canvas resisted her. How to place a blue beside a green when the world had revealed such violence in making? How to draw a human face when every face concealed an immeasurable room? She began to paint gaps: the space between two chairs, the silence between husband and wife, the dark interval between the child’s cries. These absences became her figures. Privacy, she understood, was not emptiness but depth—the deep water in which the visible life cast its wavering reflection.

Years passed through the garden. The pear tree thickened, flowered, failed, flowered again. The child grew tall and learned to close doors. Her husband’s hair silvered; his hands, once quick with buttons and laces, trembled above the teacups. They loved one another less like flame than like earth: obscurely, with roots entangled beneath what could be seen.

Then death entered without grandeur. It came as a chair left vacant, as spectacles folded beside a book, as one half of the mattress cooling toward morning. She found that grief did not roar forever. It performed small tasks. It dusted the mantel, watered the fern, set one cup upon the table and then, remembering, put the other away.

In her final painting, she made no portrait of him. She painted the house at dusk, its windows dim among the trees, and beyond it the sea—a long gray thought without conclusion. On the shore stood two figures, almost erased by distance. Between them was a narrow strip of untouched sand, luminous as secrecy, tender as a wound. Above, the first star appeared, not promising immortality, only light: ancient, belated, and still arriving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary paragraph narrated by a husband remembering his deceased wife as an enigmatic woman whose inner life always remained inaccessible to him.
counterfactuals.output: Even now, years after we lowered her into the earth, I find myself listening for the soft, deliberate tread with which she moved through our rooms, as though our house were a country she visited but never claimed. She loved me, I believe; there were mornings when her hand, resting lightly on my shoulder, seemed to say as much. Yet behind her gray eyes another life went on—a locked room lit at strange hours—and neither vows nor years nor my most patient questions ever earned me the key. Sometimes she would smile at nothing I could see, or fall silent in the middle of a song, listening inwardly to some distant bell. I knew the names of her flowers, the order of her books, the small scar beneath her wrist; I knew how she took her tea and how she feared thunderstorms. But the country of her sorrow, the source of her sudden joy, remained unmapped. Death has not made her more mysterious; it has only made me understand that mystery was the truest part of her, and that I had spent our life together standing lovingly at its shore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an early-20th-century-style meditation on a mysterious marriage, contrasting the husband’s love of untamed nature with his wife’s refined appreciation of lace, china, flowers, and beautiful objects.
counterfactuals.output:
No one in the village could quite account for their marriage. It had taken place quietly, in a pale November, when the elms were bare and the sea had the colour of pewter. He came to the church with rain on his shoulders; she, with a little veil of old Brussels lace, and a bunch of white violets trembling at her breast. They went away together under the dripping yews, and from that hour their union remained one of those facts which the mind accepts but cannot illuminate.

He loved the earth where it was least touched by man. He loved the black firs leaning before a storm, the cry of curlews over the marsh, the harsh glitter of frost on a ploughed field. At dawn he would go out alone, climbing the hills until the house below seemed no more than a white shell laid beside the dark wood. He returned with torn sleeves, burrs clinging to his coat, and that remote brightness in his eyes which belongs to those who have conversed with wind and distance.

She feared the hills a little. Their vastness oppressed her; the wind disordered her hair. Her delight was in things rescued from confusion and made delicate by human hands. She knew the separate virtues of lace—what was Flemish, what Venetian, what patiently wrought by some forgotten woman beside a narrow window. She loved thin china through which the light passed like milk; silver boxes, painted fans, bowls with blue dragons; and flowers, not scattered wildly in a meadow, but gathered into clear glass, each stem considered, each colour answering another.

Her drawing-room was a small, ordered world. In winter there were hyacinths on the table and a fire reflected in the cabinets. He would enter from the rain, bringing with him the smell of wet leaves and dogs, and stand awkwardly among her fragile treasures. Sometimes his great hand hovered above a cup as though it were a moth he dared not touch. She, watching him, would smile; yet beneath her smile there was often a faint wonder, almost sorrow.

For what had drawn them together? Perhaps each perceived in the other a country forever forbidden. To him she was civilisation in its tenderest form: the cool room after the wilderness, the white hand that placed one rose in a porcelain vase. To her he was the world before it had been trimmed and named—the forest beyond the garden wall, dangerous, shadowed, full of an inhuman freedom.

They spoke little of love. Such words would have seemed too definite for the obscure fidelity between them. In the evenings she bent over her embroidery while he sat by the window, listening to the gale move through the trees. The lamp shone upon her silks, her cups, her quiet flowers; beyond the glass the night pressed close, immense and formless. Between those two darknesses—the wild one without and the secret one within—they kept their strange companionship.

And perhaps that was their marriage: not a reconciliation, but a threshold. He never ceased to hear the hills calling beyond her curtains; she never ceased to arrange beauty against the encroaching waste. Yet each remained beside the other, guarding what could not be shared, and loving, with a grave astonishment, what could never be understood.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a poetic stream-of-consciousness passage in which a man recalls asking his wife about life and death, only later recognizing subtle signs of her mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
I asked her once what she thought death was, and she laughed—not cruelly, but as though I had mistaken a window for a door. We were washing dishes. Evening trembled in the glass above the sink, and her hands moved through the warm water, lifting each plate like a pale moon.

Life, she said, is this.

The soap? I asked.

The holding, she said. The letting go.

I remember how I rolled my eyes, wanting an answer shaped like an answer. I wanted heaven or darkness, a corridor, a field, some bright machinery beyond the body. She only dried her hands and pressed them to my face. They were colder than I expected.

Years later, I began collecting the signs I had failed to read: the pause halfway up the stairs, her wedding ring slipping loose, the untouched coffee cooling beside the bed. How she stood longer in doorways, as if listening to someone call from another room. How birds startled her. How mirrors did not.

At the time, these were merely moments, small weather passing through the house. Only afterward did they gather into prophecy.

Now I wash one plate, one cup, one spoon. The window holds the same bruised light. Sometimes I speak to her reflection there, though it is only mine softening in the glass.

What is death? I ask again.

The room says nothing.

But in the water, my hands are holding.

And in the water, they are letting go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
